question: What is the main reason why we document patient assessments in the hospital?

options.A: Ensuring continuity of care among the healthcare team
options.B: Testing new hospital computer software systems
options.C: Fulfilling requirements for medical insurance claims
options.D: Providing evidence for prosecuting criminal cases

explanation: Great job thinking about teamwork! Clear notes ensure that every nurse and doctor on duty knows the patient's current condition and treatment plan across different shifts. [learn more](GNS113_U2_T6#GNS113_U2_T6_h1)

question: How can poor documentation put a patient in danger during shift handovers?

options.A: Doctors will be forced to discharge the patient early
options.B: Critical changes in patient status may go unnoticed
options.C: Pharmacy staff will refuse to dispense routine medications
options.D: The hospital will automatically lose its accreditation status

explanation: Spot on! If notes are messy or missing, the incoming shift won't know about vital changes, which can lead to missed warning signs. [learn more](GNS113_U2_T6#GNS113_U2_T6_h1)

question: Legally speaking, if you perform a nursing action but forget to write it down, how is it viewed in a court of law?

options.A: It requires verbal testimony from the patient to prove
options.B: It is assumed another healthcare worker completed the task
options.C: It is legally considered as care that was never performed
options.D: It is classified as a minor administrative oversight

explanation: Remember the golden rule of nursing: if it wasn't charted, legally it wasn't done! Courts only trust what is written in the records. [learn more](GNS113_U2_T6#GNS113_U2_T6_h2)

question: Why is it a serious professional mistake to chart a nursing task before you have actually done it?

options.A: It falsifies the actual timeline and truth of patient care
options.B: It prevents the charge nurse from assigning tasks to aides
options.C: It causes delays in the hospital billing department workflow
options.D: It increases the physical volume of paper files in storage

explanation: You've got this! Charting ahead of time ruins the true timeline of care and misrepresents what is really happening with the patient. [learn more](GNS113_U2_T6#GNS113_U2_T6_h2)

question: Which of these is an example of objective data you collect during a physical assessment?

options.A: Complaints of dizziness upon standing up
options.C: Feeling of anxiety about upcoming surgery
options.D: Patient report of severe sharp chest pain

explanation: Objective data is what you can measure or see yourself, like vital signs. What the patient tells you is subjective! [learn more](GNS113_U2_T6#GNS113_U2_T6_h3)

question: A patient tells you, 'I feel very weak this morning.' How should you classify this information?
explanation: Spot on! Since it's something the patient feels and reports to you directly, it's subjective data because you can't measure it directly with an instrument. [learn more](GNS113_U2_T6#GNS113_U2_T6_h3)

question: What is the correct way to fix a mistake when writing in a paper nursing record?

options.A: Apply liquid correction fluid over the mistake and rewrite neatly
options.B: Draw a single line through the error and write 'mistaken entry'
options.C: Scratched out the words completely until they are unreadable
options.D: Tear out the entire page and rewrite the complete shift report

explanation: A single line lets everyone still read the original mistake while making it clear it was a correction. Never use Tipp-Ex or scribble it out completely! [learn more](GNS113_U2_T6#GNS113_U2_T6_h4)

question: Why should you avoid writing judgmental phrases like 'patient is uncooperative' in your nursing notes?

options.A: They take too much time to write during busy ward shifts
options.B: They are subjective opinions rather than measurable observations
options.C: They violate federal drug administration prescribing rules
options.D: They are automatically flagged by hospital billing computers

explanation: Always stick to the facts! Describe the exact behavior you see instead of using labels, which keeps your notes professional and fair. [learn more](GNS113_U2_T6#GNS113_U2_T6_h4)

question: In the SOAP charting format, what does the letter 'P' stand for?
explanation: Easy peasy! SOAP stands for Subjective, Objective, Assessment, and Plan. [learn more](GNS113_U2_T6#GNS113_U2_T6_h5)

question: What is the main idea behind Charting by Exception (CBE) in the ward?

options.A: Every single routine nursing action must be written out in paragraphs
options.B: Doctors review and sign nursing notes only at the end of the month
options.C: Patients write their own medical notes during hospital admission
options.D: Nurses only document findings that fall outside standard normal limits

explanation: CBE saves time by assuming everything is normal unless you specifically write down an abnormal finding. [learn more](GNS113_U2_T6#GNS113_U2_T6_h5)

question: Why is it dangerous to chart a nursing procedure that was actually performed by your colleague?

options.A: It prevents the patient from receiving their scheduled meals
options.B: It causes confusion in the hospital payroll accounting department
options.C: You cannot legally or accurately verify care you did not personally witness
options.D: It violates hospital policies regarding equipment maintenance

explanation: You can only vouch for what you saw and did yourself. Charting for others puts your own nursing license at risk! [learn more](GNS113_U2_T6#GNS113_U2_T6_h6)

question: A nurse waits until the very end of a long 12-hour shift to write down morning vital signs from memory. What kind of error has happened here?

options.A: Violation of the hospital pharmacy dispensing policy
options.B: Unlawful delegation of professional assessment duties
options.C: Delayed documentation leading to potential memory errors
options.D: Failure to use the Charting by Exception format

explanation: Human memory can be tricky after hours of busy ward work! Always try to document vital signs and assessments close to the time you take them. [learn more](GNS113_U2_T6#GNS113_U2_T6_h6)

question: Which of these actions goes directly against patient privacy and data security rules?

options.A: Shredding outdated paper assessment worksheets in a designated bin
options.B: Sharing your electronic health record password with a colleague to save time
options.C: Locking the computer screen before walking away from the nursing station
options.D: Discussing clinical findings inside a private consultation room with doctors

explanation: Your password is your digital signature. Never share it with anyone, because whatever they do on that account will legally be traced back to you! [learn more](GNS113_U2_T6#GNS113_U2_T6_h7)

question: How do regulations like the Nigeria Data Protection Regulation (NDPR) affect how we handle nursing records?

options.A: They mandate strict protection and lawful handling of patient health data
options.B: They allow patients to change their vital sign readings without nurse approval
options.C: They require hospitals to print all patient notes in English and local languages
options.D: They eliminate the need for paper records by replacing them with social media

explanation: Spot on! Data protection laws are there to make sure patient information remains safe, private, and seen only by the right healthcare staff. [learn more](GNS113_U2_T6#GNS113_U2_T6_h7)
